title: Sikhism, Jainism, Confucius and the Dao
bigQuestion: How do Sikhs, Jains, Confucians and Daoists each teach people to treat others and the world?

story.title: Everyone Sits on the Floor
story.kicker: At a Sikh gurdwara, a free meal teaches a lesson about who is equal.
paragraphs: It is Sunday morning at a gurdwara in the Chicago suburbs. A gurdwara is a Sikh house of worship. Priya's family takes off their shoes at the door. Everyone covers their head with a scarf or a turban. Priya ties a bright blue scarf over her hair.

Inside, people listen to hymns sung from a large book resting under a cloth canopy. Then they walk to a big hall. Long mats cover the floor. Volunteers are carrying pots of lentils, rice and warm flatbread called roti.

A man in a business suit sits down. Next to him sits a woman who just finished a night shift. A family visiting for the first time sits down too. Nobody has a better seat. Everyone sits on the floor in rows and is served the same food.

Priya's job today is to hand out roti. "Why is it free?" asks a visitor. Priya grins. "This is langar," she says. "Guru Nanak taught that everyone is equal. So everyone eats together, and anyone is welcome."
In this chapter you will meet four traditions. Sikhs share the langar. Jains try to harm no living thing. Followers of Confucius honor family and teachers. Daoists try to live in harmony with nature.
story.think: Why might sitting on the same floor matter more than just giving people free food?

lessons.title: Guru Nanak's Message
lessons.mainIdea: Sikhs follow the teachings of Guru Nanak, who taught one God and the equality of all people.
reading: Sikhism began in the Punjab region of South Asia about 500 years ago. Its first teacher was *Guru Nanak*, born in 1469. Sikhs tell that as a young man he went into a river and was gone for three days. When he came back, he said, "There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim."

Sikhs understand this to mean that God sees all people as one family. Guru Nanak taught that there is one God. He taught that all people are equal, whatever their religion, caste or gender. A *Guru* is a teacher. Sikhs honor ten human Gurus, from Guru Nanak to Guru Gobind Singh.

The word Sikh means learner or student. Sikhs try to remember God, work honestly and share with others. Today there are about 25 to 30 million Sikhs. Most live in India. Many live in Canada, Britain and the United States.

words.d: a teacher; Sikhs honor ten human Gurus and their holy book as Guru
a follower of Sikhism; the word means learner

look.title: The Opening of the Sikh Scripture
look.text: There is one Creator. Truth is its name. It is without fear and without hate. It is timeless and was never born.
look.cite: Mul Mantar, opening of the Guru Granth Sahib, by Guru Nanak, in our own words
look.prompt: What words in this line describe what Sikhs believe about God?

check.q: Who was the first Sikh Guru?
check.why: Guru Nanak, born in 1469, was the first Guru.

check.q: What does the word Sikh mean?
check.why: Sikh means learner.

check.q: What did Guru Nanak teach about people?
choices: Each religion has its own God
check.why: Guru Nanak taught one God and the equality of all people.

lessons.title: The Gurdwara and the Langar
lessons.mainIdea: In the gurdwara, Sikhs sing from their holy book and share a free meal called langar.
reading: A *gurdwara* is a Sikh house of worship. The name means "door of the Guru." Inside is the holy book, the *Guru Granth Sahib*. Sikhs treat it as their living Guru. It rests on a raised seat under a canopy. Hymns from it are sung with music.

Every gurdwara has a *langar*. Langar is a free kitchen and meal. Volunteers cook and serve. Anyone may eat, whether Sikh or not. People usually sit on the floor together. This shows that no one is higher than anyone else.

Visitors are welcome in gurdwaras. They cover their heads and take off their shoes. They do not bring tobacco or alcohol. The Golden Temple in Amritsar, India, is the most famous gurdwara. Its langar serves many thousands of people each day.

words.d: a Sikh house of worship; the name means door of the Guru
the Sikh holy book, which Sikhs honor as their living Guru
the free meal and kitchen at every gurdwara, open to all

look.title: Serving Langar
look.text: A volunteer rolls roti. Another stirs lentils. A girl pours water for guests. An old man washes dishes. None of them is paid. Sikhs call this seva, which means selfless service.
look.prompt: Why might Sikhs see washing dishes as part of their religion?

check.q: What is langar?
choices: a free meal open to everyone
check.why: Langar is the free kitchen and meal in every gurdwara.

check.q: How do Sikhs treat the Guru Granth Sahib?
choices: as a storybook for children only
check.why: Sikhs honor the Guru Granth Sahib as their Guru.

check.q: Why do people sit on the floor at langar?
choices: because chairs are forbidden in India
to show no one is higher than anyone else
because it is a Hindu rule
check.why: Sitting together shows the Sikh teaching of equality.

lessons.title: The Turban and the Five Ks
lessons.mainIdea: Many Sikhs keep five articles of faith, called the five Ks, and wear a turban.
reading: In 1699, Guru Gobind Singh started the *Khalsa*. The Khalsa is the community of initiated Sikhs. Members promise to keep five articles of faith. Each begins with the letter K in Punjabi. They are called the five Ks.

The five Ks are: kesh, uncut hair; kangha, a small wooden comb; kara, a steel bracelet; kachera, cotton undershorts; and kirpan, a small sword. Sikhs explain each one. The kara's circle reminds them God has no beginning or end. The kirpan stands for protecting others.

Many Sikh men, and some Sikh women, wear a *turban* over their uncut hair. The turban is a sign of faith and dignity. Sikhs in America sometimes face teasing about it. Kind classmates ask respectful questions instead.

words.d: five articles of faith kept by initiated Sikhs, each starting with K in Punjabi
a long cloth wrapped around the head; for many Sikhs a sign of faith
the community of initiated Sikhs, begun in 1699

look.title: A New Classmate
look.text: A new student named Jaspreet wears a turban and a steel bracelet. A classmate wonders about them. She could stare, or she could ask kindly at lunch: "Would you tell me about your bracelet?"
look.prompt: What is a respectful question you could ask a new classmate about their faith?

check.q: What is the kara?
check.why: The kara is one of the five Ks, a steel bracelet.

check.q: Who began the Khalsa in 1699?
check.why: Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Guru, began the Khalsa.

check.q: Which is one of the five Ks?
check.why: Kesh, uncut hair, is one of the five Ks.

lessons.title: Mahavira and Ahimsa
lessons.mainIdea: Jains follow Mahavira's teaching of ahimsa, doing no harm to any living thing.
reading: Jainism is an ancient tradition from India. Jains honor 24 great teachers called *Tirthankaras*. The most recent was *Mahavira*. He lived in India about 2,500 years ago, around the same time as the Buddha. He left his home to live a very simple life.

The heart of Jain teaching is *ahimsa*. Ahimsa means non-violence, doing no harm. Jains believe every living thing has a soul, even tiny insects. So they try hard not to hurt any being. They see ahimsa in actions, words and even thoughts.
There are about 4 to 5 million Jains today, by common estimates. Most live in India. Some live in the Chicago area. The Jain Society of Metropolitan Chicago has a temple in Bartlett.

words.d: non-violence; doing no harm to any living being
the most recent of the 24 great Jain teachers, who lived about 2,500 years ago
one of the 24 great teachers honored by Jains

look.title: A Jain Teaching
look.text: All living beings love their life. They want to be happy and do not want pain. So a person should not harm or kill any of them.
look.cite: Acaranga Sutra 1.2.3, a Jain scripture, in our own words
look.prompt: What reason does this teaching give for not harming living things?

check.q: What does ahimsa mean?
check.why: Ahimsa means doing no harm to any living being.

check.q: Who was Mahavira?
choices: the most recent of the 24 great Jain teachers
check.why: Jains honor Mahavira as the 24th Tirthankara.

check.q: Why do Jains try not to hurt insects?
choices: They believe every living thing has a soul
check.why: Jains teach that all living beings have souls.

lessons.title: Living Gently
lessons.mainIdea: Jains practice ahimsa in daily life through careful eating, speaking and working.
reading: Jains show ahimsa in many small ways. Most Jains are vegetarian. Many also avoid root vegetables, like onions and potatoes. Pulling up roots can kill tiny living things in the soil, Jains explain. Many do not eat after sunset.

Jain monks and nuns are extra careful. Some carry a soft broom to gently sweep insects from their path. Some wear a cloth over their mouth. This keeps them from breathing in tiny insects. They walk from place to place instead of riding.
Jains keep other vows too. They try to tell the truth, not steal, and not own too much. Not owning too much is called aparigraha. Jains teach that holding things lightly helps the soul become free.

words.d: a person who does not eat meat
a serious promise
the Jain vow of not owning or wanting too much

look.title: A Jain Lunch
look.text: A Jain family packs lunch in the morning. There is rice, lentils and green vegetables. There is no meat, and no onions or potatoes. They drink boiled water. They eat before the sun goes down.
look.prompt: Which parts of this lunch connect to ahimsa? Explain one.

check.q: Why do many Jains avoid onions and potatoes?
choices: Pulling roots can kill tiny living things
check.why: Jains avoid root vegetables to avoid harming small creatures in the soil.

check.q: Why might a Jain monk sweep the path gently?
choices: to move insects out of the way
check.why: The broom is a way of practicing ahimsa.

check.q: What is aparigraha?
choices: not owning or wanting too much
check.why: Aparigraha is the Jain vow of non-possessiveness.

lessons.title: Compare: Ahimsa and Karma
lessons.mainIdea: Hindus, Buddhists and Jains all speak of karma and non-harm, but in their own ways.
reading: Jainism, Hinduism and Buddhism all began in India. All three use the word karma. Jains explain karma in a special way. They describe it as fine matter that sticks to the soul. Harmful acts add more. Kind acts and self-control help clear it away.

All three traditions honor ahimsa too. Many Hindus and Buddhists are vegetarian for this reason. Jains usually make ahimsa the most central rule of all. Mahatma Gandhi, a Hindu, learned from Jain ideas. He used non-violence to work for India's freedom.

Scholars compare traditions by asking the same question of each. For example: What happens because of what we do? Each tradition answers with its own words and stories. Comparing does not mean ranking.

words.d: to look at how two or more things are alike and different
choosing not to use force or harm

look.title: Three Answers
look.text: Question: What happens because of what we do? A Hindu might say: our karma shapes our next life. A Buddhist might say: craving and actions keep the cycle of suffering going. A Jain might say: harmful actions bind karma to the soul.
look.prompt: How are these three answers alike? How is the Jain answer different?

check.q: How do Jains describe karma?
choices: fine matter that sticks to the soul
check.why: Jains picture karma as fine matter that binds to the soul.

check.q: Which leader learned from Jain ideas about non-violence?
check.why: Gandhi, a Hindu, was influenced by Jain ideas of ahimsa.

check.q: What is a fair way to compare traditions?
choices: ask each the same question and describe its answer
count which is oldest and pick it
check.why: Scholars compare by describing each answer without ranking.

lessons.title: Confucius and Respect
lessons.mainIdea: Confucius taught respect for parents and teachers and kindness as the base of a good society.
reading: *Confucius* lived in China about 2,500 years ago. His Chinese name is Kongzi, which means Master Kong. He was a teacher. He believed a peaceful society starts with good families and good leaders. After he died, his students wrote down his sayings in the *Analects*.

Confucius taught *filial piety*. That means respect and care for parents and grandparents. He also taught respect for teachers and elders. He said leaders should be good examples, not bullies. Good manners and rituals help people live well together, he taught.

Confucius's most important value is often called ren. Ren means kindness or humaneness toward others. Many families in China, Korea, Japan and Vietnam still honor his ideas. Some call Confucianism a religion; others call it a way of life.

words.d: the book of Confucius's sayings, written down by his students
respect and care for parents and elders
a Chinese teacher who lived about 2,500 years ago

look.title: A Rule for Life
look.text: What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others.
look.cite: Confucius, Analects 15.23, tr. James Legge, The Chinese Classics vol. 1 (1861)
look.prompt: Put this saying in your own words. Where have you heard a similar rule?

check.q: What is the Analects?
check.why: His students wrote down his sayings in the Analects.

check.q: What is filial piety?
choices: respect and care for parents and elders
check.why: Confucius taught filial piety, respect for parents.

check.q: What did Confucius say leaders should do?
check.why: Confucius taught that leaders should lead by good example.

lessons.title: The Dao: The Way of Nature
lessons.mainIdea: Daoists try to live in harmony with the Dao, the natural way of all things.
reading: Daoism is an ancient tradition from China. Its best-known book is the *Daodejing*. Tradition says a wise man named Laozi wrote it. Scholars are not sure who wrote it or when. It is short and full of poems about the Dao.

*Dao* means the way. Daoists describe the Dao as the natural flow behind all things. They say it cannot be fully put into words. Daoists try to live simply and not force things. They learn from water, which is soft but can wear away rock.

The yin-yang symbol comes from Chinese thought. It is a circle of dark and light that fit together. *Yin* and *yang* are opposites that need each other, like night and day. Many Daoists believe health and peace come from keeping them in balance.

words.d: "the way"; in Daoism, the natural flow behind all things
the best-known Daoist book, linked by tradition to Laozi
two opposite forces that need each other and stay in balance

look.title: Be Like Water
look.text: The best way to live is like water. Water helps all things and does not fight with them. It goes to low places others avoid.
look.cite: Daodejing, chapter 8, in our own words
look.prompt: What does water teach, according to this passage?

check.q: What does the word Dao mean?
check.why: Dao means the way, the natural flow of things.

check.q: What do yin and yang show?
choices: opposites that need each other and stay in balance
check.why: Yin and yang are paired opposites in balance.

check.q: Why do Daoists learn from water?
choices: It is only found in temples
It is soft but strong and does not fight
check.why: The Daodejing praises water for helping without fighting.

lessons.title: Lunar New Year and Blended Ways
lessons.mainIdea: Lunar New Year and ancestor honoring show how many people in East Asia blend several traditions.
reading: *Lunar New Year* falls in late January or February. It follows the moon. Families clean the house to sweep out bad luck. They share big meals and give red envelopes with money to children. Each year is named for one of twelve animals, like the dragon or the rabbit.

During the new year, many families honor their *ancestors*. Ancestors are family members who lived long ago. People may set out food or burn incense before family pictures. This practice is linked to Confucian respect for family.

In China, Korea, Japan and Vietnam, many people follow more than one tradition. A family might honor ancestors in a Confucian way, visit a Buddhist temple and use Daoist ideas about balance. Many people there do not see this as a problem. Chicago's Chinatown celebrates the new year with a parade.

words.d: a new year festival that follows the moon, celebrated in much of East Asia
a family member who lived long ago

look.title: The Animal Years
look.prompt: What animal names the year 2026? What animal comes next after the Horse?

check.q: What do children often get at Lunar New Year?
check.why: Red envelopes are a Lunar New Year custom.

check.q: Why do many families honor ancestors at the new year?
choices: to show respect for family, linked to Confucian ideas
check.why: Honoring ancestors connects to Confucian filial piety.

check.q: What is true of many people in East Asia?
choices: They follow more than one tradition at once
check.why: Many blend Confucian, Buddhist and Daoist ways.

review.q: Where does every gurdwara serve a free meal?
review.why: Langar is the free kitchen in every gurdwara.

review.q: Which tradition is best known for ahimsa to every living thing?
review.why: Jains make ahimsa their central rule.

review.q: Which book holds the sayings of Confucius?
Which book is linked to Laozi?
review.why: Tradition links the Daodejing to Laozi.

review.q: Which of these is one of the Sikh five Ks?
review.why: The kirpan is one of the five Ks.

review.q: A person honors grandparents and teachers. Which Confucian idea is this?
review.why: Filial piety is respect for parents and elders.

choices: many gods in balance with yin
one God and equality of all people
no harm to insects above all
review.why: Guru Nanak taught one God and that all people are equal.

review.q: A Jain family does not eat after sunset. Which idea explains this?
choices: ahimsa, avoiding harm to tiny beings
review.why: Many Jains avoid eating after dark to avoid harming insects.
